title: Inference hosting comms & operator-first brief
summary: Short comms brief and tactical playbook for conversations where buyers are comparing Redwood against in-house stacks built on vLLM / TGI / TensorRT-LLM. Focus: operator pain, unpredictable ops costs, time-to-production, and quality regression risks. This doc is written for sales, solutions engineering, and field marketing to use in calls, emails, and collateral.
hypothesis: Buying managed inference is primarily a risk-transfer and velocity decision for operator-heavy orgs. Engineering-first customers will test DIY because early metrics look cheap; the tipping point to purchase is when variability (latency, cost, reliability) materializes across scale, model changes, or regulated data needs.
positioning_statements: For platform engineers: Redwood is the operational abstraction that turns inference from 'something to babysit' into a measurable service with SLOs and predictable economics.
For ML engineers: Redwood preserves model iteration speed while removing the infra overhead of continual kernel tuning and batching heuristics.
For CTOs/VP Eng: Redwood de-risks customer-facing latency and cost surprises and buys a migration path without lock-in because we support the same open models and quantized variants.
For Security/Compliance: Redwood offers private deployment options and audit-ready controls so you get the benefits of managed runtime without sacrificing governance.
key_messages: Time to value beats peak theoretical cost. A working, SLAd, observable endpoint in days vs months is often worth 10–30% higher steady-state cost for the first 6–12 months.
Operator tax is the hidden multiplier: engineers maintaining vLLM/TGI clusters spend 20–40% of developer cycles on infra tuning and incident fixes — this creates opportunity cost.
We don’t just host models — we optimize the whole inference path (kernel selection, KV cache, batching, fallback routing) so teams move cost optimization off their critical path.
Fallback-first reliability: automatic model fallbacks and region routing keep customer endpoints live during upgrades and infra churn — something DIY setups rarely bake in consistently.
competitive_grid:
High-level comparison summary (verbal):
- vLLM/TGI (DIY) = Lower apparent infra bill at tiny scale, high variance in latency, high ops headcount, frequent regressions after model changes.
- TensorRT-LLM (DIY hardware-optimized) = Great per-token throughput for specific hw + model combos but very brittle across model updates and requires deep infra expertise.
- Redwood (managed/dedicated/private) = Slightly higher short-term unit cost for fast time-to-value, but lower total cost of ownership once you include ops headcount, outage cost, and rollback risk. Optimized runtime reduces unit cost gap over time through kernel tuning, caching and quantization recommendations.
battlecard_bullets: Objection: 'We can run vLLM ourselves for cheaper.' Response: Confirm scale + variability assumptions — show example where token unit cost flips when accounting for prefix caching and burst overhead; propose a short pilot to validate.

Objection: 'TensorRT gives best throughput.' Response: Agree on throughput advantage but probe on model churn and dev velocity; highlight our multi-variant fallback and automated kernel selection that preserves throughput while supporting model updates.
Objection: 'We control our data more with DIY.' Response: Outline Redwood Private deployment and KMS/HSM integrations that give parity with self-hosted controls while removing day-to-day ops.
risk_mitigation: For customers worried about lock-in: emphasize model versioning, exportable configs, and documented migration lanes back to self-hosted if they choose later.
For cost-sensitive buyers: run a 30-day side-by-side with real traffic capture and TCO analysis including engineer ops time; provide suggested batching/quantization knobs tuned to their workload.
For security-minded orgs: propose an early security review + architecture diagram and offer a private deployment pilot with limited data residency constraints.
recommended_calls_to_action: Ask for telemetry: request a 7–14 day sample of request sizes and seq len histograms — this lets us produce an immediate unit-cost and latency projection.

Propose a 4-week pilot: day 0 onboarding + day 7 baseline + day 21 cost/op removal report + day 28 go/no-go. Include rollback plan and acceptance criteria (p50/p95 latency, error budget, cost per 1M tokens).
Offer an 'ops workshop': 1–2 hour session with their infra and ML leads to map runbooks and identify immediate win lanes (4–8% unit cost improvement through caching/batching).
roi_example: Illustrative ROI (verbal): take a mid-market app doing 100M tokens/month. DIY infra (including 0.5 FTE infra + 1.0 FTE ML ops) shows direct infra $6k/mo + payroll ops $25k/mo = $31k/mo. Redwood hosted entry estimate $12k/mo (infra + managed service) + 0.2 FTE support = $15k/mo. First 6 months net savings: ~96k and faster feature releases. Numbers are illustrative; always run with customer telemetry.
pilot_plan: Step 1: Discovery (1–3 days) — gather traffic histograms, model sizes, latency SLOs, security requirements.
Step 2: Quick onboarding (1 week) — ingest a snapshot of traffic into a sandbox, enable prefix caching and one recommended quantization profile.
Step 3: Production shadow (2 weeks) — mirror traffic, compare latency and unit cost under identical load; run chaos (node restarts) to show fallback behavior.
Step 4: Readout + decision (1 week) — deliver a cost/latency/regression report and recommended next steps (dedicated capacity vs private deployment).
open_questions: What threshold of ops FTE or minutes of downtime triggers procurement for customers in our top segments?
Which cloud regions + custom hardware do our largest competitors commonly run on, and how does that affect our demo scripts?
Can we create a short automated sampling tool that customers can run to produce the 14-day telemetry bundle we ask for?
